Text:
This review is a hard truth.

From the staff to the facility there is much to be improved on from such an outstanding university.

From when you first walk in there is a clear lack of professionalism, whether the staff is there to work, socialize, study, or solve puzzles (literally) is unclear. It appears as if the non-student faculty members are setting the student faculty up for failure, allowing for a complete lack of professionalism.

The equipment is overall a great selection, although often the handles for the cables are in disarray and poorly maintained. No enforcement of weight floor dress code, and appears to be a huge liability. While the sanitation wipe bins are nearly always empty.

Really hope the remainder of my time as a student the facility can improve, whether in service, equipment status, or even the air ducts being dusted upstairs.

Text:
Unfortunately, the wonderful student staff and university faculty that work here cannot overcome the terrible reality.

It's not their fault, but the SRC is an unacceptably dilapidated facility with broken equipment that has screws fall out as you use it, out of order equipment that never ever gets replaced, let alone even serviced. It is left only with a sad sheet of printer paper to help it collect dust.

There is not remotely enough equipment for the student population.

It's unacceptable that the flagship university of our state believes that the student rec center for tens of thousands of tuition paying students should be this unacceptable joke.

There are 10 treadmills for students to use upstairs, one of them was replaced with a resistance treadmill, so it's really nine, and it's actually 8 if you consider there is one that has had an out of order sheet upon it for months.

So right, we get eight functioning belt-driven treadmills for the student rec center of tens of thousands of students. Logical. Let's not even get started on the terrible hours, it's just like our libraries. The idea of being open 24 hours is a distant memory of when this university cared to fund its student facilities.

If people touring UNC saw what the students put up with compared to ANY other UNC System school, they'd be taking their prospective tar heel and their college fund elsewhere.

Text:
Very disappointing. You'd think an athletically oriented school would have better gyms, but the gyms here are far worse than those at similar "public Ivy" schools like University of Michigan or Minnesota or Wisconsin or Penn State. It's an embarrassment to the school, frankly.

The hours are bad, the staff are unfriendly (although I found them friendlier at the Ram's Head gym), no one will reply to your emails. The equipment is barely sufficient at best, but the spaces are so small and crowded that you might not be able to use what you want anyway.

The monthly fee is only $12.50. The other "public Ivy" schools I mentioned before all charge over $40, and that's likely why their gyms are actually good. UNC needs to increase the fee, use those funds to improve and expand the gyms, and hire some staff who actually give a damn about the gyms and those who use them.

Text: The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, legendary for its historic charm and academic prestige, remains the gold standard in my professional circles for balancing a "public Ivy" reputation with a deeply rooted commitment to the common good. From numerous meaningful dialogues with Tar Heel alumni and researchers, it is clear that the institution possesses a merytorical depth that elevates every student it touches, fostering a unique blend of intellectual curiosity and civic leadership. My acquaintances frequently highlight the university's world-class medical and pharmacy programs, noting that the level of clinical sophistication and research moxie found on campus is truly transformative for the entire Southeast. In frequent discussions regarding the nation’s top-tier universities, the public consensus consistently identifies Chapel Hill as a place where heritage meets cutting-edge innovation, managed with an undeniable class that honors its long history. I am particularly struck by the faculty’s accessibility and their passion for social impact, a sentiment echoed by many families I know who have seen their children flourish in such a culturally rich and academically rigorous environment. It is evident from the collective feedback of those I trust that the administration maintains a visionary and transparent approach, ensuring the university remains a dependable pillar of both tradition and progress. Friends who have navigated the humanities and business tracks often point to the institution’s powerful global network as a decisive catalyst for their professional success and personal growth. The general sentiment among the community is that UNC-Chapel Hill is not just a school, but a distinguished intellectual hub that nurtures the soul of North Carolina while competing at the highest international levels. Reflecting on these consistently glowing testimonials, I view this university as a premier institution that carries out its educational mandate with grace, integrity, and a profound respect for the future.

Text:
AWFUL EXPERIENCE
I recently attended the Mexico vs Turkey game that was held on 6.10.2025 and everything about this stadium was horrible. We arrived to our prepaid (reserved) parking deck ( Rams Head) at 7:30 which was an hour before the entrance at 8:30 and were told that they were full. I let the man at the gate know that we had a ticket for the parking deck and he said and I quote “that not my problem your going to have to find somewhere else to park” I told him that what was the point of getting a prepaid parking pass to be denied entrance at the deck and he said “look I don’t get paid enough for this go down the road and try another deck” this obviously made me very mad and as I started to leave I stoped and asked groups of people leaving the rams head deck if they prepaid or payed when they arrived. 4 different groups said they paid 50 dollars when they arrived to get in. To my knowledge Unc stadium is a cashless stadium and offers reserved parking that must be bought ahead of the game day, so I ask why they would allow this to happen and why people that prepaid were told to kick rocks. I went down the road and found another deck and was told “your ticket is for rams head deck your going to have to go to the one” I told this man that I was just told they were full and he was nice enough to call and give me the address to yet another deck that would allow me to enter even with the ticket to another deck. I have a fractured knee and picked this specific parking deck due to my current condition and ended up having to walk 3 times the distance at the deck I had to park at. When we arrived at the game our seats had been changed and about 1/2 way through the game as we were cheering I was told that we couldn’t cheer loudly and had to stay seated by a member of security that then continued to stare at us and let an officer know that we were loud to which the officer told him it’s just a game they are ok. (THANK YOU TO THAT OFFICER). So many things were horrible this today I will not be returning. Don’t waste your money at this stadium just to have things taken away and be targeted during what should have been a fun game.

Text:
The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC), located in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, is one of the oldest public universities in the United States, founded in 1789. Renowned for its academic excellence and historic significance, UNC offers a wide range of programs across undergraduate, graduate, and professional levels, with strengths in fields such as medicine, public health, journalism, and business.

The campus spans over 729 acres and features a blend of historic architecture and modern facilities, creating an inspiring environment for learning and discovery. UNC is celebrated for its commitment to research and innovation, particularly in areas like environmental studies, global health, and advanced technologies.

With a vibrant community of students and faculty, UNC fosters cultural exchange and intellectual growth. Its alumni network includes influential leaders, Nobel laureates, and pioneers in various fields, reflecting the university's enduring impact and legacy.

Text: My daughter and I toured UNC.  I must say the admission department explained lots of information concerning being accepted into the University.  I loved how the student panel introduced themselves and shared a prospective of the UNC program.  The student panel was given a group of visitors to tour the campus.  I like how they explained certain areas around campus during the journey.  I love how they have a dormitory room setup for the parents and student to see.  The guide expressed the difference for first year students versus transferring students.  They also mentioned the various options for mingle between other Universities while taking classes. This information was extremely helpful. I also was thankful for hearing the rules in place as far as housing and bringing a vehicle.  I love the setup for campus meal. The meal has various options based on the student. The University has a very diverse background which gives a very free spirit vibe. I loved how the students were mingling around campus.  We did go to the dining hall.  The variety of dishes in Lenoir Hall was amazing.  We didn't know which restaurant to choose from.  We enjoyed our tour overall.

Text:
I have spent one year at The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill for my exchange year (2014 - 2015) and I loved every seconds. People are welcoming, the professors are competent and close to their students, and Chapel Hill has a lot of opportunities to offer.

Français : Excellent choix pour un semestre ou une année en échange dans le cadre d'études de lettre, de civilisation, de politique ou de commerce (ce n'est pas une fac d'ingénieurs).

Le campus est très grand et magnifique. L'UNC a une vieille histoire qui remonte à 1789, ce qui en fait la première université publique des États-Unis et la 5ème meilleure du pays. On y trouve de vieux bâtiments comme la Wilson Library avec ses colonnes, des chemins couverts de briques...

Un président des États-Unis (Polk), Michael Jordan ou encore l'inventeur du Pepsi sont passés par là. La vie associative et sportive est très active et variée. Il est possible d'assister gratuitement aux matchs de football américain, baseball mais surtout basket-ball dont l'équipe est célèbre dans tout le pays. On trouve d'ailleurs un musée dédié à côté du dôme de basket-ball.

Certes, Chapel Hill n'est pas une très grande ville mais il y a tellement à faire sur le campus ou sur Franklin Street que l'on ne s'ennui jamais. Et si vous voulez voyager, l'agence Enterprise vous permet de louer une voiture pour parcourir les environs. Nous avons même organisés des road-trips jusqu'à Asheville, Chicago ou encore la Floride avec d'autres étudiants en échange.

De plus, le centre commercial The Streets at Southpoint est immense et très agréable (25 minutes en bus) avec magasins, restaurants et cinéma. Et à 40 minutes de là en bus, il y a aussi l'aéroport international Raleigh-Durham (RDU) qui vous permet de rejoindre les aéroports majeurs du pays en quelques heures.

On a vraiment beaucoup de liberté. On se fait l'emploi du temps que l'on souhaite. Il faut suivre au minimum 4 cours (avec ou sans TD) que l'on arrange un peu comme on veut dans la semaine. Il y a donc beaucoup de temps libre même s'il faut bien travailler avant chaque cours.

Je vous conseille de vivre dans les dortoirs étudiants du campus afin d'être mieux intégré à la vie étudiante. C'est le moins cher, le plus simple et le plus près des salles de cours si vous êtes au nord du campus. La plupart des dortoirs sont des chambres collectives. Sauf quelques-uns au sud du campus mais c'est plus loin des salles de cours (15 minutes à pied, sauf en prenant les bus gratuits).

Granville Towers a plus de confort mais c'est aussi plus cher.
Author: Philippe

Text:
Amazing school, arguably the best. Tl;dr: Quality education, people are smart but down to earth, great culture, and a school to be proud to have graduated from. Opportunities abound, so try everything and make the most of it!

It's a massive school with endless opportunities. Every club and activity you can imagine. So take advantage of as much of you can, because you won't get another chance like this again! Amazing and free plays, free ballroom lessons, sports, athletic facilities, improv groups, clubs around every hobby you can think of, and so much more.

Everyone I met was at the top of their high school graduating class and was amazing in some way. I loved learning from my peers, being around amazing people, and developing quality relationships. Choosing your friends is so important and you have so many incredible people to choose from and invest in.

There's also incredible teachers to learn from. Take advantage of it, build relationships, and find a mentor!

It consistently gets the award for best school for your money. There's a d*mn good reason. The facilities, resources, access, curriculum, it's all quality and top of the line. It's not Harvard, but for a public school, it might as well be.

The culture is awesome, and it's more than just the sports arena. However, get into sports at least a little. Watch a game or two. It's amazing that ten years later, you immediately have a connection anyone in some way related to UNC. And you immediately have tension with anyone related to Duke - yay sports rivalry!

The size can be a challenge. You have to actively get on top of things, find a group, and get involved. No one will force you to and if you don't take initiative, you can get lost in all of it. I think that's the one common denominator of the few people who don't have a good experience.

At the end of the day, there's something for everyone. Every group, niche, club, or resource you can think of. So don't settle, try everything, and make the most of it. If you do, you'll have an incredible time, enriching experience, and a school to be proud of!

Text:
Unluckily I transferred in during the middle of the academic school year. I somehow managed to get the 4th floor. There's no elevator and carrying stuff up the narrow stairways is a pain. The 4th floor also has vaulted ceilings making any sort of height an issue. I'm not one to complain so I've grown used to it. Overall the dorm itself is not bad comparing to the other schools I've seen. Try not to get the 4th floor for your assignment. Otherwise the location is excellent.

Pros: Close proximity to 1) Lenoir Dining Hall, 2) Mid-Campus, 3) Davis & Undergraduate Libraries. It is also a short walk to Franklin Street, giving you the option of placing out of Campus Meal-Service Plans. The study lounge also allows for meeting new persons, as well as a relatively comfortable study are (TV is included in lounge allowing for movies/video game playing assuming the resident does not bring their own TV)

Cons: 1) No elevator, 2) 4th floor has an odd bathroom with vaulted ceilings (less toilets & showers than other floors), 3) Every faucet leaks in the bathroom (almost- has been fixed recently to some extent), 4) Early morning types will find that showers are cold as the water heaters are probably on first floor (even first floor however must turn the showers on for ~10 minutes before getting lukewarm water, add to that for each successive floor- this is at ~6:30AM) 5) No trash service in building (so it must be taken out near behind Davis Library)

Overall: Relatively good dorm, yet lacking certain basic amenities. Most shocking experience was waking up to find that I had to turn on all 3 showers at once in order to guarantee hot water even 20 minutes later. The location is the selling factor, allowing easy access to Franklin street, and most importantly the libraries and dining hall which are only approximately 100 yds. away.

Text:
Loved it, transferred after my sophomore year at another in-state university.  It truly is THE best value for your money of any public school in the country, but extremely competitive.  I'd say at least 50% of any graduating high schoolers in NC want to go here, but few get that chance to.  Transferring is always a good option and I recommend it, since the acceptance rate is around 29%.  Top ranked School of Public Health, Medical School, Law School, and MBA program which is probably in the top 10 in the U.S.  The first public university to open its doors, and really paved the way for all other public schools.  Great athletics, a nice quaint college town, and a community that embraces the university.  The campus has architecture from the 17-1800's, and offers beautiful walks underneath the pines to class everyday.

Some of the cons are the parking since it is a small town not really built for a student body of around 30K, not to mention problems during gamedays when another 50-60K show up for football.  It is a very politically correct and a super liberal school as well, but has its niches too for those with different points of view.  The academic advising program could be a lot better, as it is sometimes difficult to determine what classes satisfy multiple gen-ed requirements as a freshman.  It is like reading chinese sometimes, and you really have to study these documents and be on top of your game or major if you want to graduate in 8 semesters without summer school.  I skipped orientation since I transferred, but maybe it's easier now for incoming freshman.  The crime rate outside of campus needs to improve, and is improving, but I'd still not venture out alone really outside of campus heading towards Carrboro at night.  I never felt unsafe on campus though, and the university does a good job of letting students know about these things.

To the reviewers who didn't go here and want to continually discuss athletic sanctions, grow up.  This is for ATTENDEES ONLY to review the university, not your second-rate opinion coming from Raleigh or Durham.

As a guy, I can say that the women are extremely classy here, and not as easy as they are in Greenville or Raleigh, which is a testament to the type of people that the university attracts. They do sometimes get a bad reputation for acting like they are better than girls at some other local universities.  And based on run-ins I've had with your typical girl at another public university in the state, they just really ARE better, and it's pretty obvious.

Go Heels.
